bio.en: Dan Shipper is co-founder and CEO of Every, a 15-person company building four products at the bleeding edge of what's possible with AI, with a head of AI operations automating the team's workflows.
bio.zh: Dan Shipper 是 Every 的联合创始人兼 CEO，这家仅 15 人的公司在 AI 可能性的最前沿打造了四款产品，并设有 AI 运营负责人来自动化团队工作流。

summary.en: Dan shares how his team operates at the edge of AI adoption, with a head of AI operations constantly building prompts and workflows that the whole team automates. He argues entry-level jobs aren't being taken—kids with ChatGPT will simply move far faster—and that organizations playing at the edge today are doing what everyone else will in three years. The conversation is a window into a near-future way of building companies.
summary.zh: Dan 分享了团队如何在 AI 应用的最前沿运作——设有 AI 运营负责人不断构建提示词与工作流，全员自动化。他认为初级岗位并未被夺走——用 ChatGPT 的孩子只会快得多——而今天在边缘探索的组织，正做着别人三年后的事。对话是一扇窥见“近未来公司运作方式”的窗口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The business you're building, the team you're building, the way you're operating is the very bleeding edge of how companies are trying to operate in this AI era.
turns.zh: 你正在建立的业务、你正在建立的团队、你的运营方式都是公司在这个人工智能时代如何运营的最前沿。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: We have a head of AI operations. She's just constantly building prompts and building workflows that I and everyone else on the team are just automating as much as possible.
turns.zh: 我们有一位人工智能运营主管。她只是不断地构建提示和构建工作流程，我和团队中的其他人都在尽可能地实现自动化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some things that you believe about AI that most people don't?
turns.zh: 关于人工智能，有哪些你相信但大多数人不相信的事情？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I hate the headlines that are like, "Entry-level jobs are taken away by AI." Whenever I see a kid with ChatGPT, I'm like, "Holy shit, they're going to go so much faster than any other person that I've worked with." We have this guy, he made a year's worth of progress in two months because every time I sat down with him and told him, "Okay, here's how you tell a story, here's how you think about a headline," he recorded all of it, put it into a prompt, and he never made the same mistake twice.
turns.zh: 我讨厌“初级工作被人工智能夺走”之类的头条新闻。每当我看到一个使用 ChatGPT 的孩子时，我都会想，“天哪，他们会比我共事过的任何其他人都快得多。”我们有一个人，他在两个月内取得了一年的进步，因为每次我坐下来告诉他，“好吧，这就是你如何讲一个故事，这就是你如何思考一个标题，”他记录了所有这些，将其放入提示中，并且他从未犯过两次同样的错误。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this sense we're getting to a place where you don't have to write any code, you have a product team not writing code at all.
turns.zh: 有一种感觉，我们正在到达一个不需要编写任何代码的地方，您的产品团队根本不编写代码。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: No one is manually coding anymore. Organizations like ours, people who are playing at the edge, we're doing things that, in three years, everybody else is going to be doing.
turns.zh: 没有人再手动编码了。像我们这样的组织，那些处于边缘的人，我们正在做的事情，在三年内，其他人都会做。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Thank you for having me. I've obviously been a huge fan for a long time and so it's an honor to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你有我。显然我长期以来一直是它的忠实粉丝，所以很荣幸来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my honor, Dan. I feel like this is a podcast that was meant to be. I'm so happy we're finally doing this. There's so damn much that I want to talk about; there's so damn much we can talk about. I thought it'd be fun to start with just some hot takes. (00:04:29): And the reason I want to start here is I feel like you spend more time thinking about AI, building with AI, using AI, evaluating AI than anyone else I know nearly. And so I really respect your insights and your perspectives on where things are going. So let me just ask you this question and see where this goes. What are some things that you believe about AI using AI tools that most people don't believe?
turns.zh: 这是我的荣幸，丹。我觉得这就是一个注定的播客。我很高兴我们终于做到了这一点。我想说的事情实在是太多了；我们有太多可以谈论的事情了。我认为从一些热门镜头开始会很有趣。 (00:04:29)：我想从这里开始的原因是我觉得你比我认识的任何人都花更多的时间思考人工智能、利用人工智能构建、使用人工智能、评估人工智能。所以我真的很尊重你对事情发展的洞察力和观点。所以让我问你这个问题，看看会发生什么。关于使用人工智能工具的人工智能，您相信哪些事情是大多数人不相信的？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I'm going to go with my hottest take, and this is the take that I have the least evidence for. So let's just start with that. I have other more well-reasoned takes to give you, but this is my hottest one, which is I think that AI may be one of the biggest force for reshoring American jobs. And so I think everyone is worried about it unemploying people. And for sure, it will change the skills needed to do the jobs that you're doing, but I think it may actually reshore a lot of jobs, and it'll do that in two ways. (00:05:27): One is, there are a lot of expensive services that rich people and big companies are paid for right now, so in-house counsel or call center or whatever. And what cheap intelligence does is it makes those kinds of things affordable for small companies and individuals. So it stimulates demand. The other thing that it does is it allows people who are in those jobs to serve more people cheaply. It may not get rid of customer service, for example, but it may allow 10 people in the Midwest, who would normally be working at a call center, to serve hundreds of thousands or millions of people. Maybe that's too much, but a lot more people than they would ordinarily if they were the ones on the phone all the time. (00:06:22): And so it becomes much more cost-effective for American companies to hire people in the US. And I think the people in the US are going to be better, in a lot of cases, at using these AI tools to do work. So I think it may actually make it more effective to have those jobs in the US run by people sitting in the US who are using it to get work done. And also, the model companies are here too. So there's a lot of American stuff happening, and you can decide whether or not you think that's a good thing, but I think it's quite lost in the conversation over whether AI will get rid of jobs.
turns.zh: 我将选择我最热门的观点，而这是我拥有最少证据的观点。那么我们就从这个开始吧。我还有其他更合理的观点可以给你们，但这是我最热门的观点，即我认为人工智能可能是美国就业岗位回流的最大力量之一。所以我认为每个人都担心失业。当然，它会改变你正在做的工作所需的技能，但我认为它实际上可能会重新安排很多工作，并且会通过两种方式做到这一点。 (00:05:27)：一是，现在有很多昂贵的服务是富人和大公司付费的，所以内部咨询或呼叫中心等等。廉价情报的作用是让小公司和个人买得起这些东西。所以它刺激了需求。它所做的另一件事是，它允许从事这些工作的人以低廉的成本为更多的人服务。例如，它可能不会取消客户服务，但它可能允许中西部的 10 名通常在呼叫中心工作的人员为数十万或数百万人提供服务。也许这太多了，但如果他们一直打电话的话，人数会比平时多得多。 (00:06:22)：因此，美国公司在美国雇用员工变得更具成本效益。我认为在很多情况下，美国人会更好地使用这些人工智能工具来工作。因此，我认为，让美国的人来管理这些工作，并利用这些工作来完成工作，实际上可能会更有效。而且，模特公司也在这里。因此，美国发生了很多事情，你可以决定你是否认为这是一件好事，但我认为在人工智能是否会消除工作的对话中，人们完全迷失了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like optimistic takes about AI, so this is great. And to your point, TBD if this is good for other countries, but good for the US. What else? What else you got? What other hot takes?
turns.zh: 我喜欢对人工智能持乐观态度，所以这很棒。就你的观点而言，这是否对其他国家有利，但对美国有利，尚待确定。还有什么？你还有什么？还有哪些热点？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Okay. Another big hot take, and this is less contrarian and more just, I think, people are truly sleeping on it. I think people are truly sleeping on how good Claude Code is for non-coders. And I'll extend this to not just Claude Code, but Google just came out with the Gemini CLI command-line interface. So things like that. And I'll tell you for people who are listening that don't know what Claude Code is. Claude Code is just the command-line interface. It's those black terminals that programmers use. It's a command-line interface that you can boot up. It has access to your file system, it knows how to use any kind of terminal command and it knows how to browse the web, all that kind of stuff. (00:07:47): You can give it something to do and it will go off and it'll run for 20 or 30 minutes and complete a task autonomously, agentically. Especially with Claude Opus 4 that just came out, it's this gigantic leap forward in AI's ability to work by itself. And Claude Code can even spawn multiple sub-agents that do a bunch of tasks in parallel and it's incredibly useful for programmers. Everybody inside of Every is using it all day, every day. Everyone's agent-pilled. They've got 15 agents doing all this kind of stuff. It's crazy. (00:08:18): But non-programmers don't use it because it's intimidating to use the terminal. But for example, you can download all your meeting notes and put it in a folder and just be like, "Okay, I want you to read every single one of my meeting notes and tell me..." Something that I do, for example, is, "Tell me all the time that I subtly avoided conflict." (00:08:38): And it writes a little to-do list for itself. It can have a little notebook, it can go and read each little thing and then write into its notebook, go down its to-do list and give you a summarized answer over multiple turns. So it's not just stuffing everything into context, which is what you'd be doing with ChatGPT chat or a regular Claude chat. It's actually processing every single file that you give it. And so I think it's incredibly powerful for any kind of task that involves processing a lot of text.
turns.zh: 好的。另一个热门观点，我认为，这不那么逆反，更公正，人们真的在睡觉。我认为人们确实在沉迷于 Claude Code 对于非编码人员来说有多好。我不仅将其扩展到 Claude Code，而且 Google 刚刚推出了 Gemini CLI 命令行界面。诸如此类的事情。我会告诉你那些不知道克劳德·科德是什么的听众。 Claude Code 只是命令行界面。这就是程序员使用的那些黑色终端。这是一个可以启动的命令行界面。它可以访问您的文件系统，它知道如何使用任何类型的终端命令，它知道如何浏览网页，等等。 (00:07:47)：你可以给它一些事情做，它就会启动并运行 20 或 30 分钟，并自主、代理地完成任务。尤其是刚刚发布的 Claude Opus 4，这是人工智能独立工作能力的巨大飞跃。 Claude Code 甚至可以生成多个子代理来并行执行大量任务，这对于程序员来说非常有用。 Every 内部的每个人每天都在使用它。每个人都被代理了。他们有 15 名特工在做所有这些事情。太疯狂了。 (00:08:18)：但是非程序员不会使用它，因为使用终端会让人感到害怕。但是，例如，您可以下载所有会议记录并将其放入一个文件夹中，然后说：“好吧，我希望您阅读我的每一份会议记录并告诉我......”例如，我所做的事情是，“一直告诉我我巧妙地避免了冲突。” (00:08:38)：它为自己写了一个小待办事项列表。它可以有一个小笔记本，它可以阅读每一件小事，然后写入笔记本，记下待办事项列表，并在多次轮流中给你一个总结的答案。因此，这不仅仅是将所有内容都填充到上下文中，这就是您在 ChatGPT 聊天或常规 Claude 聊天中所做的事情。它实际上正在处理您提供给它的每个文件。因此，我认为它对于任何涉及处理大量文本的任务来说都非常强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So as a simple way to think about this, you basically have an agent on your local computer that can read your local files and do your bidding.
turns.zh: 因此，作为一个简单的思考方式，您的本地计算机上基本上有一个代理可以读取您的本地文件并执行您的命令。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yes, exactly. And it can do that for long amounts of time without going off the rails.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。而且它可以在很长一段时间内做到这一点而不会偏离轨道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. And so there's a small hurdle that non-technical people have to overcome, which is using their terminal and giving commands, but once they get it running, it's just you talk to it in English and ask it to do stuff.
turns.zh: 有趣的。因此，非技术人员必须克服一个小障碍，即使用终端并发出命令，但是一旦他们让它运行，您只需用英语与它交谈并要求它做一些事情即可。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the hot take here is just Claude Code, which most people think is for engineers, is the most underrated tool for non-technical people.
turns.zh: 所以这里最热门的就是 Claude Code，大多数人认为它是针对工程师的，对于非技术人员来说是最被低估的工具。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some other ways you imagine people seeing this? This meeting note example is really cool and I could see people using this. What else have you seen or thinking about?
turns.zh: 您想象人们会以哪些其他方式看到这一点？这个会议记录示例非常酷，我可以看到人们使用它。您还看到或想到了什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Something that I've done a lot, so I'm a writer for a lot of my job. And I know you're going to ask me about books I love, so I'm going to give you a sneak peek, which is I love War and Peace. I just read it for the third time.
turns.zh: 我已经做了很多事情，所以我的很多工作都是作家。我知道你会问我我喜欢的书，所以我要给你先睹为快，那就是我喜欢《战争与和平》。我刚刚读了第三遍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's a long book.
turns.zh: 哇，这是一本很长的书。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: It's so long, but it's so good. I think Tolstoy is a brilliant writer. And one thing that I wanted to do is I was like, "I want to inflect some of my writing with some of Tolstoy's style." And the way I did that is I think he's incredible at these little subtle sentences where he shows you what a character is thinking and feeling just by how they behave, how they move their face or the mismatch between the intonation in their voice and the expression in their eyes, all that kind of stuff. He's just an incredible student of human behavior and psychology. (00:10:36): And so I just downloaded War and Peace to my computer, which you can do because it's public domain. And then I had Claude read the first three chapters of War and Peace and pull out all of those descriptions, and then make a guide for itself for how to do character descriptions like Tolstoy. And you could totally do this with a regular Opus command, but you couldn't put all of War and Peace into it. It would take a lot more hand holding to get it to do this. And it just did this by itself without my really intervening. (00:11:05): I had it download a Russian version of War and Peace and the English version, and then start comparing different scenes that I love to tell me about things that I might've missed in the translations, so that you can get as deep and weird and nerdy for whatever subfield you care about as you want to. Same thing for if you've got tons of customer interviews or tons of customer data you want to go through, it's incredibly powerful for going and figuring stuff out from big data sets like that.
turns.zh: 虽然这么长，但是真的很好啊。我认为托尔斯泰是一位出色的作家。我想做的一件事是，“我想用托尔斯泰的一些风格来改变我的一些写作。”我这样做的方式是，我认为他对这些微妙的小句子的表现令人难以置信，他通过角色的行为方式、他们的面部表情、声音的语调和眼睛的表情之间的不匹配，向你展示了角色的想法和感受，诸如此类。他是人类行为和心理学方面令人难以置信的学生。 (00:10:36)：所以我刚刚将《战争与和平》下载到我的计算机上，您可以这样做，因为它是公共领域。然后我让克劳德读了《战争与和平》的前三章，取出所有这些描述，然后为自己制作一个指南，指导如何像托尔斯泰那样进行人物描述。你完全可以用常规的 Opus 命令来做到这一点，但你不能把《战争与和平》的全部内容都放进去。需要更多的帮助才能做到这一点。它只是自己完成了这件事，没有我的真正干预。 (00:11:05)：我让它下载了《战争与和平》的俄语版本和英语版本，然后开始比较不同的场景，我喜欢告诉我在翻译中可能错过的事情，这样你就可以按照你想要的方式对你关心的任何子领域进行深入、怪异和书呆子的了解。同样的事情，如果你有大量的客户访谈或大量的客户数据你想浏览，它对于从这样的大数据集中找出东西来说是非常强大的。

turns.zh: 我认为他们绝对会的。我还认为模型公司可能会开始让这变得更容易理解。我认为 Claude Code 和其他类似的东西将出现在你使用的所有其他东西中，无论是在网络上还是在其他地方，其中一件事就是所有原始的人工智能应用程序都将聊天框粘贴到现有的 UI 中。现在您已经有了 Copilot，它在 IDE 中具有自动完成功能。你有光标，它有一个带有一些聊天功能的小侧边栏。与 Claude Code 的不同之处在于你从不看代码。它不适合编码，也不适合手动编码。 (00:13:34)：它的意思是让你说：“我希望你完成某件事”，然后它就会去做。我认为我们已经到了这样一个阶段，对于几乎所有常见的应用程序来说，人工智能都将足够好，我们可以或多或少地摆脱界面，你可以深入研究它实际上正在做的所有事情，你可以与它的执行交错​​，你更像是，“我正在授权，它会去做它。”

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I have one other hot take, which is I have a definition for AGI. And so AGI is famously hard to define. What does it mean for it to be artificial general intelligence? The Turing test was one, but we'd pretty much blown past the Turing test in a lot of ways. So we have no good one. And so what I have noticed is that you can tell how much better AI is getting by how long a leash you can give it to do work. (00:15:09): So with Copilot, you can tab complete and that was the beginning. With ChatGPT, you ask it a question and it returns a response and that's maybe slightly better than a tab complete. And then now with Claude Opus 4 and Gemini and all that kind of stuff, also with deep research, it can go off and work for 20 or 30 minutes. So that leash is getting longer where you have to intervene. (00:15:34): And I was thinking about this and it reminded me of Winnicott, who was a child psychologist. He wrote this book called Playing & Reality. And his conceptualization for what it means to become an adult, what it means to go from being an infant to a child to an adult is when you're first born, you're effectively fused with usually your mother, your caregiver. There's no difference between you and her or you and whoever your caregiver is. (00:16:02): And growing up is this process of being gradually let down in certain moments where you can handle being let down. So you learn that there's a separation between you and your caregiver. So for infants, it's instead of being fused at the hip for every hour of every day, you get left alone. Maybe you get left alone to cry it out. Who knows if that's the right thing to do with infants? A lot of consternation there. But that's teaching you that there's a separation between you and your mom or you and your dad. There's not going to always be someone to pick you up. (00:16:38): And raising a child is about knowing when they're ready to be let down a little bit and have to stand up on their own. So I think there's that same leash with human development. You get longer and longer periods of time where you can be on your own. So we're still in the 20 to 30 minutes is maybe... I don't know, you probably can't leave a toddler alone for 20 or 30 minutes, but it's a little bit older than a toddler.
turns.zh: 我还有另外一个热门观点，那就是我对 AGI 有一个定义。因此众所周知，AGI 很难定义。通用人工智能意味着什么？图灵测试就是其中之一，但我们在很多方面都远远超过了图灵测试。所以我们没有好的。所以我注意到，你可以通过限制人工智能工作的时间长度来判断人工智能的进步程度。 (00:15:09)：因此，使用 Copilot，您可以按 Tab 键完成操作，这就是开始。使用 ChatGPT，您向它提出问题，它会返回响应，这可能比选项卡完成稍好一些。现在有了 Claude Opus 4 和 Gemini 以及所有类似的东西，也经过深入研究，它可以启动并工作 20 或 30 分钟。因此，在你必须干预的地方，皮带变得越来越长。 (00:15:34)：我在思考这个问题，这让我想起了温尼科特，他是一位儿童心理学家。他写了一本名为《游戏与现实》的书。他对成为成年人意味着什么，从婴儿到儿童再到成年人的概念化是，当你第一次出生时，你通常与你的母亲、你的照顾者融合在一起。您和她或者您和您的照顾者之间没有区别。 (00:16:02)：成长就是在某些时刻逐渐感到失望的过程，在这些时刻你可以处理失望。因此您了解到您和您的看护者之间存在分离。因此，对于婴儿来说，你不是每天每个小时都在臀部融合，而是独自一人。也许你会被留下独自哭泣。谁知道这对婴儿来说是否正确？那里有很多惊愕。但这告诉你，你和你妈妈或者你和你爸爸之间存在着分离。不会总是有人来接你。 (00:16:38)：抚养孩子就是要知道他们什么时候准备好感到失望并必须自己站起来。所以我认为人类发展也有同样的束缚。你可以独处的时间越来越长。所以我们可能还剩下 20 到 30 分钟……我不知道，你可能不能让一个小孩独自呆 20 或 30 分钟，但它比一个小孩大一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe 20, 30 seconds.

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: With a toddler, you can be in the same room but not interacting with them every single second for 20 minutes sometimes. So it's around there. I think we have that similar leash with AGI. And so I think a good definition of AGI is when does it become economically profitable for people to run agents indefinitely? So it just never turns off. It's a Claude Code that's always running, it's always doing something, you just never turn it off, and you don't need to because you know that it's worthwhile to keep it on. (00:17:41): It's never waiting for you to be like, "Okay, next thing." It'll always respond to you when you're like, "Okay, next thing." But it's off just essentially living its life like a teenager and that is profitable for you. You'd rather have it do that than just wait for you to tell it what to do next.
turns.zh: 对于幼儿，您可以在同一个房间里，但有时不能在 20 分钟内每时每刻都与他们互动。所以它就在那里。我认为我们对 AGI 也有类似的约束。因此，我认为 AGI 的一个很好的定义是，人们何时可以无限期地运行代理来获得经济利益？所以它永远不会关闭。这是一个始终在运行的克劳德代码，它总是在做一些事情，你只是永远不会关闭它，而且你也不需要这样做，因为你知道保持它打开是值得的。 (00:17:41)：它永远不会等你说“好吧，下一步。”当你说“好吧，下一步”时，它总是会回应你。但它本质上只是像青少年一样生活，这对你来说是有利可图的。你宁愿让它这样做，也不愿等你告诉它下一步该做什么。

turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 有趣的。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I think that's a good definition of AGI.
turns.zh: 我认为这是 AGI 的一个很好的定义。

turns.en: It's partly the cost and partly the value. And obviously, you can game this a little bit and be like, "Cool, I'm just going to tell Claude to run in a loop forever." And I like the profitable thing, because if it costs a little bit of money and the bar is profitability, it has to actually be doing something useful for you to keep it on.
turns.zh: 部分是成本，部分是价值。显然，你可以玩一点游戏，然后说：“酷，我只是要告诉克劳德永远循环运行。”但我谈论的不仅仅是这些，更广泛地采用始终有效的代理。我喜欢有利可图的事情，因为如果它花费一点钱并且盈利能力是标准，那么它必须实际上做一些对你有用的事情才能保持下去。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I have plenty of them. I hate the headlines that are like, "It's going to replace jobs," or "It's going to unemploy two thirds of the workforce." I don't think that's true. I hate headlines that are like, "You don't use your brain when you use ChatGPT," or another good headline is, "Doctors alone, doctors plus AI, or just AI, which one is better? AI is better, therefore, doctors are going to be outmoded." (00:19:18): All that stuff is, I think, pretty dumb. So for the doctors plus AI example, I think it's important to recognize that using AI is a skill. And so if you study doctors in a vacuum that don't really have a lot of experience with AI, you could probably create a situation such that it's better to just use an AI. And sometimes it is going to be better. But there's so many contexts that doctors need to make decisions and do things that it's really hard to take one study and make any conclusion about that. (00:19:52): And it's especially hard when you're dealing with a technology that's developing so rapidly that doctors can't really be expected to be experts at it yet. But I would guess in five or 10 years, that will be totally and completely different. For the student example or the "AI turns your brain off" example, I think it's really important to understand that in the history of technology, it has always been the case that you give up certain skills in order to get other ones. For example, Plato is famously very skeptical of writing because he thought it would harm your memory. And it did. We don't remember things quite as well as they did back in the day because they had to remember long epic poems to entertain each other. (00:20:37): But I think writing is a worthwhile trade for having a slightly worse memory. And I think something similar is going on with AI where you may be slightly less engaged in certain tasks, but if you use it right, you're going to be way more engaged in other tasks where you have much more power. And so you can construct a study that says brain connectivity goes down when you use AI in the same way that you could construct a study that says people's memory are worse when they have writing skills. But I don't think anyone would want to go back to a world where no one was literate.
turns.zh: 我有很多。我讨厌诸如“它将取代工作”或“它将导致三分之二的劳动力失业”之类的头条新闻。我不认为这是真的。我讨厌这样的标题，“当你使用 ChatGPT 时，你没有使用你的大脑”，或者另一个好的标题是，“单独的医生，医生加人工智能，或者只是人工智能，哪个更好？人工智能更好，因此，医生将会过时。” (00:19:18)：我认为所有这些东西都很愚蠢。因此，对于医生加人工智能的例子，我认为重要的是要认识到使用人工智能是一种技能。因此，如果你在真空中研究那些在人工智能方面没有太多经验的医生，你可能会创造一种情况，即最好只使用人工智能。有时它会更好。但医生需要做出决定和做事情的情况太多了，因此很难通过一项研究并就此得出任何结论。 (00:19:52)：当你处理的技术发展如此之快，以至于医生还不能真正成为该领域的专家时，这尤其困难。但我猜五年或十年后，情况将会完全不同。对于学生的例子或“人工智能让你的大脑关闭”的例子，我认为理解这一点非常重要：在技术史上，你总是会为了获得其他技能而放弃某些技能。例如，众所周知，柏拉图对写作非常怀疑，因为他认为写作会损害你的记忆。确实如此。我们记事的能力不如以前的他们，因为他们必须记住长篇史诗才能互相娱乐。 (00:20:37)：但我认为对于记忆力稍差的人来说，写作是一项值得的交易。我认为人工智能也会发生类似的情况，你可能会稍微少参与某些任务，但如果你正确使用它，你会更多地参与其他你拥有更多权力的任务。因此，你可以构建一项研究，表明当你使用人工智能时，大脑连接性会下降，就像你可以构建一项研究，表明人们在拥有写作技能时记忆力会变差一样。但我认为没有人愿意回到一个没有人识字的世界。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super interesting. There's all these studies that are showing the benefits of AI to students with these studies in Nigeria and just how fast people progress. So I think it's really important, this context you're sharing that you will lose some things, but the hope is the gain is much higher, and so far it seems like it will be.
turns.zh: 那是超级有趣的。所有这些研究都通过尼日利亚的这些研究向学生展示了人工智能的好处以及人们进步的速度。所以我认为这非常重要，你所分享的这个背景你会失去一些东西，但希望收获会更高，到目前为止似乎会如此。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah. I think people always, especially at the beginning of a tech hype cycle or a revolution paradigm shift, it's always easy to underestimate how quickly things are going to change. And the example I always use is, I live in Brooklyn and the tailor down the street from me doesn't accept credit cards. Credit cards have been around for a long time, so it takes a long time for technology like this to be adopted even in the best case. (00:21:55): And I think it's really easy to underestimate how complex specific contexts are that humans know how to deal with. And just because you can get a really good score on a test... It's incredible. I love AI, it's so incredible, but it doesn't actually give you an intuition for how difficult it is to actually be replacing specific parts of work or activities that you would do. I think a really good thing to give you maybe a little bit of an intuition for it is I built this thing over a weekend a month ago that was, "0.3, can it predict what I'm going to say in a meeting?" (00:22:45): That's a benchmark. It's the CEO benchmark. And the reason I did that is because the gold standard for OpenAI for testing how powerful a model is, is they test it on their internal code base. So they say, "How good is the new model at predicting what comes next in our internal code base?" Because that's not anywhere out on the internet. So it's a really good benchmark for that. And so I was like, "Well, my meeting transcripts aren't anywhere on the internet. A lot of what I say is on the internet and there's some overlap, but it'd be interesting." (00:23:19): And so I ran a bunch of the frontier models on this, on just my Granola transcripts, and they're pretty bad. They are pretty bad, and it's not because they're not smart. There's this real push now. Tobi from Spotify coined this term called "context engineering," which is getting the context to the model, the right context at the right time, is at least half the performance. (00:23:43): And I think that's 100% true. It's something that I've been writing about for three years. At the time, I called it knowledge orchestration. turns.en: Super interesting. And they just keep a file or they put this into a project? Is that how they store this stuff?

turns.zh: ...他们可以互相分享。 (00:44:24)：他们做的另一件事，我认为非常酷，是他们同时使用了一群克劳德，但随后他们还使用了其他三个特工。他们喜欢一个叫星期五的特工。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 那是一个叫星期五的AI亚洲产品？

turns.zh: 他们非常喜欢另一个叫查理的人。特别是，我认为他们喜欢查理的一点......我们有一个关于此的完整视频，我可以将其发送给您。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'll point to it.
turns.zh: 是的，我会指出它。

turns.en: They did an S-tier through F-tier of AI agents, which I think is so funny. And that seems to work really well to have different agents that have maybe slightly different perspectives. It's like different people that have different perspectives and have different taste. (00:45:15): Kieran, he's one of those serious Rails-files, who they just love Rails, and they love the way that Rails feels, and so I think he has a real sensitivity to... Okay, this agent, ChatGPT for example, it feels very terse, and minimal, and professional, and it has a particular kind of style that maybe he likes. Versus, I don't know, Claude is a slightly different style. And I think all of that is so interesting that these things have personalities, and that that changes what you might want to use it for or why you might want to use three of them at once.
turns.zh: 他们做了 S 级到 F 级的人工智能代理，我认为这很有趣。我真正喜欢 Charlie 的原因之一是它位于 GitHub 中，因此当你收到拉取请求时，你可以对 Charlie 说：“你能检查一下吗？”对于拥有可能略有不同观点的不同代理人来说，这似乎非常有效。就像不同的人有不同的观点和不同的品味一样。 (00:45:15)：Kieran，他是那些严肃的 Rails 文件之一，他们只是喜欢 Rails，他们喜欢 Rails 的感觉，所以我认为他对……好吧，这个代理，例如 ChatGPT，感觉非常简洁、简约、专业，而且有一种他可能喜欢的特殊风格。对比一下，我不知道，克劳德的风格略有不同。我认为所有这些都很有趣，这些东西都有个性，这会改变你可能想要使用它的用途，或者为什么你可能想要同时使用其中三个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so fascinating. It makes me think about Peter Deng's conversation again, where he talks about his hiring strategy and one of his key lessons. And he ended up hiring the current head of product for ChatGPT, the current head of marketing at ChatGPT, the current head of engineering because he hires these incredible people. (00:46:07): And his philosophy is to hire a team of Avengers, where everyone is strong at certain things, and together they're the perfect team, versus everyone... versus the best at everything. And it's interesting that you can almost do that with different product, different agents from different companies.
turns.zh: 那真是太迷人了。这让我再次想起 Peter Deng 的谈话，他谈到了他的招聘策略和他的重要教训之一。他最终聘请了 ChatGPT 现任产品主管、ChatGPT 现任营销主管、现任工程主管，因为他雇用了这些令人难以置信的人才。 (00:46:07)：他的理念是雇佣一支复仇者联盟，每个人在某些事情上都很强大，而且他们在一起就是完美的团队，与每个人对抗......与所有事情上最优秀的人对抗。有趣的是，您几乎可以使用不同公司的不同产品、不同代理商来做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: You definitely can.
turns.zh: 你绝对可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it makes me feel like there's a bigger market than people think potentially, where people will want different companies, agents, not just all Devins or not all Codexes.
turns.zh: 这让我觉得有一个比人们想象的更大的市场，人们会想要不同的公司、代理商，而不仅仅是所有的 Devins 或不是所有的 Codex。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I think there really is. It's definitely not one agent to rule them all at all.
turns.zh: 我想确实有。绝对不是一个代理人可以统治他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting.
turns.zh: 太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, my God. The two people on the Cora team, what's their background? Are they both engineers or what are they?
turns.zh: 我的天啊。 Cora团队的这两个人，他们的背景是什么？他们都是工程师还是什么？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: They're both engineers.
turns.zh: 他们都是工程师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Kieran's got this crazy background, where... They both have really interesting backgrounds. Kieran's got this crazy background, where he was previously VP Eng at a startup, so was effectively the CTO of a startup, or maybe two startups, and was one of the founders. But before that, he was a composer, a professional composer. And before that, he was a baker. So we did a team retreat in France last year, and he taught us all how to make croissants. My croissant was horrible. His was beautiful.
turns.zh: 基兰有一个疯狂的背景，他们都有非常有趣的背景。 Kieran 有着疯狂的背景，他之前是一家初创公司的工程副总裁，因此实际上是一家初创公司（或者可能是两家初创公司）的首席技术官，并且是创始人之一。但在此之前，他是一名作曲家，一名职业作曲家。在此之前，他是一名面包师。所以去年我们在法国进行了一次团队静修，他教我们所有人如何制作牛角面包。我的羊角面包很糟糕。他的很漂亮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Seems [inaudible 00:47:16].

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: And generally, I think that kind of multidimensional type of talent is the kind of person that I love having at Every. Because we're all generalists. We all want to use AI for all these weird, awesome, creative things. And someone who has that background is going to have a good taste for not only agents, but, "What should the landing page look like," or whatever. Which I think is increasingly important, where you're trying to scale a team of generalists of 15 people to five products. So that's Kieran's background. (00:47:43): Natasha's background is... I'm jealous because he only started learning to code when ChatGPT came out. He had wanted to learn to code forever, and he's only known how to code in an AI era. And I keep telling him, "Dude, I learned to program in middle school from books." I had to go to Barnes & Noble and buy a book. And there was nothing... I couldn't Google any-
turns.zh: 总的来说，我认为这种多维度的人才是我喜欢在 Every 拥有的那种人。因为我们都是多面手。我们都想用人工智能来做所有这些奇怪的、很棒的、有创意的事情。具有这种背景的人不仅会对代理有良好的品味，而且会对“登陆页面应该是什么样子”或其他什么有很好的品味。我认为这一点越来越重要，因为您正试图将 15 人的通才团队扩展到五种产品。这就是基兰的背景。 (00:47:43)：Natasha 的背景是……我很嫉妒，因为他是在 ChatGPT 出现时才开始学习编码的。他一直想永远学习编码，而他只知道在人工智能时代如何编码。我一直告诉他，“伙计，我在中学时从书本上学会了编程。”我不得不去巴诺书店买一本书。什么也没有...我无法谷歌任何-

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I had to go to Barnes and Noble and buy a book and there was nothing... I couldn't Google anything about why this function wasn't working.
turns.zh: 我不得不去巴诺书店买一本书，但什么也没有……我无法用谷歌搜索任何关于为什么这个功能不起作用的信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No Stack Overflow even back then.
turns.zh: 即使在那时也没有堆栈溢出。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. There wasn't that overflow. There was weird BB net forums and stuff that I was like 12 and I probably shouldn't have been on there or whatever. So he has gone so much faster than any other engineer, I think in a pre AI era. And I see the same thing in the rest of the company. I think there's this huge question about what happens when kids... Entry level jobs are taken away by AI. And my take is like that's worth thinking about and it's possible that that might be a problem at some point. But my take is whenever I see a kid with ChatGPT, I'm like, holy shit, they're going to grow so much faster than any other person that I've worked with. We have this guy Alex Duffy who works with us, he writes for Context Window and he just launched, we taught AIs how to play diplomacy with each other, which is really cool. (00:49:08): And he did that whole thing and I think he's really, really, really talented. And when he came to us, I guess almost a year ago now, it was one of those classic cases which I've seen over and over at every... Which is, you have great ideas, but you're not a good writer yet and it's really hard for me to do anything with you until you're good enough at it. So I have to give you small little things until you get better and blah, blah, blah, whatever. And what I noticed with him is he was just making a year. He made a year's worth of progress in two months because every time I sat down with him and told him, okay, here's how you tell a story. Here's how you think about a headline. He recorded all of it, put it into a prompt, and he never made the same mistake twice. (00:49:49): And I think he's so much accelerated from where he would have been because of this stuff, and I see that in lots of other parts of the work. So Natasha is another good example. And so I think generally people are going to figure out that some 20-year-old with ChatGPT subscription is super powerful if you just mentor them. And I think that's great.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。没有那种溢出。有一些奇怪的 BB 网论坛和我 12 岁时可能不应该参加的东西。所以我认为在前人工智能时代，他比任何其他工程师都快得多。我在公司其他部门也看到了同样的情况。我认为，当孩子们的入门级工作被人工智能夺走时，会发生什么是一个巨大的问题。我的看法是，这值得思考，而且在某些时候这可能会成为一个问题。但我的看法是，每当我看到一个使用 ChatGPT 的孩子时，我就会想，天哪，他们的成长速度比我共事过的任何其他人都要快得多。我们有一个亚历克斯·达菲（Alex Duffy）和我们一起工作，他为 Context Window 撰稿，他刚刚推出，我们教人工智能如何相互玩外交，这真的很酷。 (00:49:08)：他做到了这一切，我认为他真的非常非常有才华。当他来到我们这里时，我想差不多一年前了，这是我一遍又一遍地看到的经典案例之一……也就是说，你有很棒的想法，但你还不是一个好的作家，在你足够擅长之前，我很难和你一起做任何事情。所以我必须给你一些小事，直到你好起来，等等，等等，等等。我注意到他才刚刚赚了一年的钱。他在两个月内取得了相当于一年的进步，因为每次我和他坐下来告诉他，好吧，这就是你讲故事的方式。以下是您对标题的看法。他把这一切都记录下来，放入提示中，而且他从来没有犯第二次同样的错误。 (00:49:49)：我认为，由于这些东西，他比原本应该达到的位置加速了很多，而且我在工作的许多其他部分中看到了这一点。娜塔莎是另一个很好的例子。所以我认为一般来说，如果你指导一些订阅了 ChatGPT 的 20 岁年轻人，他们会变得非常强大。我认为这很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, there's so many threads I could follow here. There's all this fear of entry level people will never... The roles are disappearing for entry level people and so how will we ever have senior people if these people can't learn to do things as an entry level person? And what you're saying is ChatGPT and these tools help you accelerate really quickly so you don't really need to be at the bottom rung for a long time.
turns.zh: 伙计，这里有很多我可以关注的话题。对于入门级人员的所有这些恐惧永远不会......对于入门级人员来说，这些角色正在消失，所以如果这些人不能学会像入门级人员那样做事情，我们将如何拥有高级人员呢？您所说的是 ChatGPT，这些工具可以帮助您快速加速，因此您实际上不需要长时间处于底层。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah. You're effectively learning how to be one level above the entry level from the beginning and this is sort of my whole allocation economy thesis where when you look at skills are going to be valuable in the AI era, one big group of skills are the skills of managers. Today, they're human managers, tomorrow everyone's a model manager. Right now, AI is not... Right now, management skills are not broadly distributed, because it's very expensive, another expensive thing that... So 8% of the workforce is managers. It's now going to be much cheaper to manage, so more people are going to have to do it. And so that's the thing that kids, 20-year-olds, whatever, I see is now are going to start to have to learn in addition to, it's not like you can just say, okay, go do it and then come back. You have to be able to go into the work that's being done and help make it better. But they're learning both at the same time. They're learning how to manage and how to do the actual work so that they're good at it.
turns.zh: 是的。你正在有效地学习如何从一开始就比入门级高出一个级别，这就是我的整个分配经济论文，当你看到技能在人工智能时代将变得有价值时，一大群技能就是管理者的技能。今天，他们是人力经理，明天每个人都是模范经理。现在，人工智能还没有……现在，管理技能还没有广泛分布，因为它非常昂贵，另一个昂贵的东西……所以8%的劳动力是经理。现在管理成本将大大降低，因此更多的人将不得不这样做。所以我认为，这就是孩子们、20 岁的人，无论什么，现在都必须开始学习的东西，而且，你不能只是说，好吧，去做，然后再回来。你必须能够投入到正在完成的工作中并帮助它变得更好。但他们同时学习两者。他们正在学习如何管理以及如何做实际工作，以便他们擅长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the managing here is managing agents. Right?
turns.zh: 这里的管理就是管理代理。正确的？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah. You're managing AI.
turns.zh: 是的。你正在管理人工智能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so coming back to your point about how this core team, and I guess you said everyone doesn't write code, zero code written, now it's just managing agents that are writing code for you.
turns.zh: 回到你关于这个核心团队的观点，我猜你说过每个人都不写代码，零编写代码，现在只是管理代理为你编写代码。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I've never heard of a company at this stage, so this is extremely cool. So the workflow is they give it, here's what I want. I refine it using this cool prompts library that they build on and agents build code, write the code. Then basically the time is spent reviewing code and then reviewing the output. What does it look like? What does it feel like? And then continuing to refine, wow. So you guys are at where Michael from Cursor said we will be. So I chatted with him a few months ago. He said in a year, this is where he thinks the thing will be. We're not looking at code anymore. You guys are already there. Although you were looking at code. Okay, you're still looking at code.
turns.zh: 好的。我在这个阶段从未听说过一家公司，所以这非常酷。所以工作流程是他们给的，这就是我想要的。我使用他们构建的这个很酷的提示库来完善它，代理构建代码，编写代码。然后基本上时间花在审查代码，然后审查输出上。它看起来像什么？感觉如何？然后继续完善，哇。所以你们现在已经到达 Cursor 的 Michael 所说的位置了。所以几个月前我就和他聊过。他说，一年后，这就是他认为事情会发生的地方。我们不再看代码了。你们已经在那里了。尽管您正在查看代码。好吧，你还在看代码。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: They definitely are looking at code. So you're doing a code review before you do anything. And I do think Danny, who runs Spiral, which is the cloud code for content tool I was talking about that we're building, he spent a couple of days digging into the internals of some third party library that we were interested in just because it's helpful to know, it's helpful to understand those things, but then he's not actually writing any code. Once he understands it, he's just off telling cloud code what to do. And I think that's really important.
turns.zh: 他们肯定是在看代码。所以你在做任何事情之前都要进行代码审查。我确实认为，运行 Spiral 的丹尼（Spiral）是我正在谈论的我们正在构建的内容工具的云代码，他花了几天时间深入研究了我们感兴趣的一些第三方库的内部结构，只是因为了解这些内容很有帮助，理解这些东西很有帮助，但他实际上并没有编写任何代码。一旦他理解了，他就会告诉云代码该做什么。我认为这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is an insane milestone we're hitting here. There's this sense we're getting to a place where you don't need to really understand code, you don't have to write any code. We'll get there and you guys are there. I think this is so easy to overlook how wild this is. You have a product team not writing code at all.
turns.zh: 这是我们在这里达到的一个疯狂的里程碑。有这种感觉，我们正在到达一个不需要真正理解代码、不需要编写任何代码的地方。我们会到达那里，你们也在那里。我认为这很容易让人忽视它的疯狂程度。您的产品团队根本不编写代码。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: It is really wild. I think it's really wild in particular, just having a small group of people that have... Everyone has all these different skills. Everyone's a generalist, everyone's AI forward. So what you can do in an environment like that with just still a small team is crazy. And you're kind of inventing all these new principles for how do we work together, how do we do engineering, all that kind of stuff. And I think that's what makes the writing... That's why I like doing that is because the writing that we do from that I think is really good because we can talk about it from a sort of position of experience, but I do want to say something else which is we're not at a point yet where the people that work at every could do what they do if they didn't know how to code.
turns.zh: 真的很狂野。我认为这真的很疯狂，只有一小群人……每个人都有不同的技能。人人都是多面手，人人都是AI前锋。因此，在这样的环境中，只有一个小团队就能做的事情是疯狂的。你正在发明所有这些关于我们如何合作、如何进行工程以及所有此类事情的新原则。我认为这就是写作的原因……这就是为什么我喜欢这样做，因为我认为我们所做的写作真的很好，因为我们可以从某种经验的角度来谈论它，但我确实想说点别的，那就是我们还没有达到这样一个地步：如果每个地方工作的人不知道如何编码，他们就可以做他们所做的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, this is what I was going to ask.
turns.zh: 是的，这就是我想问的。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Which is a different bar, and I think for a long time it's going to be valuable to know how to code for a long time, but this is a progression that is not a new progression. So for example, when I was in middle school learning to code, the new hot thing was scripting languages, which is Python and JavaScript. But if you were a real programmer, you would understand the language underlying Python and JavaScript, which is written in C. and scripting language weren't totally real. And in order to really do anything interesting, you had to be able to learn both parts of the stack. Same thing for C programmers, when I guess in the seventies C was invented, it was like you got to be able to write assembly. (00:54:59): And English is just a layer on top of scripting languages. So I think all of those things were right in the sense that there's... Especially during transitions, there's a lot of reasons why it's important to be able to go down a layer in the stack and it gets less and less frequent over time, but that still takes a long time. And there's some times when even if you're a JavaScript or a Python programmer, it's useful to know how that stuff works, how it's written, and see how it's implemented. Today it's much less important than it used to be, but that took 10 or 20 years. And I think that the same thing is going to be true for programming. Having that skill is super important and will accelerate you significantly. It will sort of start to get less important over time, but we're not close to that yet.
turns.zh: 这是一个不同的酒吧，我认为在很长一段时间内，长期了解如何编码将是有价值的，但这是一个进步，而不是一个新的进步。例如，当我在中学学习编码时，新的热门事物是脚本语言，即 Python 和 JavaScript。但如果你是一个真正的程序员，你就会理解 Python 和 JavaScript 的底层语言，它是用 C 编写的。脚本语言并不完全真实。为了真正做一些有趣的事情，你必须能够学习堆栈的两个部分。对于 C 程序员来说也是如此，我猜当 C 语言在七十年代发明时，就好像你必须能够编写汇编语言一样。 (00:54:59)：英语只是脚本语言之上的一层。所以我认为所有这些事情都是正确的，因为……特别是在转换期间，有很多原因可以解释为什么能够在堆栈中向下一层很重要，并且随着时间的推移它会变得越来越不频繁，但这仍然需要很长时间。有时，即使您是 JavaScript 或 Python 程序员，了解这些东西如何工作、如何编写以及如何实现也是很有用的。如今，它的重要性已不如以前，但这花了 10 年或 20 年的时间。我认为对于编程来说也是如此。拥有这项技能非常重要，并且会显着加快你的速度。随着时间的推移，它会开始变得不那么重要，但我们还没有接近这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That's a really important point. I'm glad you went there. So do you have a sense of how far we might be from you hiring someone to build another product that isn't an engineer?
turns.zh: 好的。这是非常重要的一点。我很高兴你去了那里。那么，您是否知道我们距离您聘请非工程师的人来构建另一种产品还有多远？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Like a real SaaS product?
turns.zh: 喜欢真正的 SaaS 产品吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So hey, we have this idea we want to bring someone on to actually lead it.
turns.zh: 所以，嘿，我们有这个想法，我们想找人来真正领导它。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Very far. Not within sight, but there's a lot of things that could be products that are a level down from that I think that you could do almost now. So an example, we were talking about DIA, the new AI browser from the browser company. DIA has these things called skills, which are effectively little AI apps that you can run in the browser. You can prompt them and they run on the web page and do work for you. A non-technical person can build that, same thing for custom GPTs from ChatGPT. A non-technical person can definitely build that. So I think while I will definitely maintain that we're not anywhere close to anybody being able to build a conventional SaaS app with zero programming knowledge, aside from just a demo, there are going to be other forms of software. (00:56:55): One of my things is like software is becoming content. There's going to be other forms of software that don't look like the software today, but you can run, start and run as a business, as a non-technical person even if you don't know how to code. And that'll happen very soon. I mean, it's already kind of happening. It doesn't look like the thing that you're asking about. It's sort of like the difference between a Hollywood movie and a YouTube video.
turns.zh: 很远。虽然还看不到，但有很多事情可能是比我认为你现在几乎可以做的产品低一个级别的产品。举个例子，我们正在谈论 DIA，浏览器公司推出的新型人工智能浏览器。 DIA 有一些称为技能的东西，它们实际上是可以在浏览器中运行的小型人工智能应用程序。您可以提示它们，它们会在网页上运行并为您工作。非技术人员可以构建它，对于来自 ChatGPT 的自定义 GPT 也是如此。非技术人员绝对可以构建它。因此，我认为，虽然我肯定会坚持认为，我们还没有任何人能够用零编程知识构建传统的 SaaS 应用程序，但除了演示之外，还会有其他形式的软件。 (00:56:55)：我的一件事就是软件正在成为内容。将会有其他形式的软件看起来不像今天的软件，但即使您不知道如何编码，您也可以作为企业、作为非技术人员来运行、启动和运行。这很快就会发生。我的意思是，这已经发生了。它看起来不像你要问的问题。这有点像好莱坞电影和 YouTube 视频之间的区别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's really reassuring to a lot of people. Basically what you're seeing is AI just supercharges people who have a skill and allows them to do a lot more.
turns.zh: 我认为这确实让很多人感到放心。基本上你所看到的是人工智能只是增强了拥有技能的人的能力，让他们能够做更多的事情。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Is there any other way that you guys operate that is really interesting that might be worth sharing that helps you operate really quickly, helps you do more with less?
turns.zh: 好的。你们还有其他真正有趣、值得分享的操作方式吗？它可以帮助您快速操作，帮助您事半功倍？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I mean, I would love to talk about how we think about building products, what products to build, what do we end up building? Because I think that there's something sort of special about it that probably there's a playbook that is useful for people. So when I think about... This is only sort of snapped into focus recently. So a lot of this was just doing it intuitively without really a thought for it. But when I think about the kind of things that we have ended up incubating, it's basically goes back to something I said at the beginning, which is there are these things that were historically really expensive that only rich people or big companies could buy. So a chief of staff for your email, I think a therapist or a lawyer is another interesting example. Someone to organize your closet or organize your computer is another example. Someone to go straight for you, that are becoming orders of magnitude cheaper so that everyone can use them even if you're at a small startup. (00:58:39): And so basically when you're running, we are sort of this AI first company. You're running into all these little things where you're like, I wish I had a ghost writer right now, but ghost writers are really expensive. Or I wish I had a lawyer but it would cost me like $25,000. Lawyers are really expensive and there's a lot more demand for those services than can be fulfilled because they're so expensive. And what AI does is it allows you to be like, oh, I could just use cloud for that. I can use ChatGPT for that. And so you're able to use the demand that you have that we can afford a lawyer. We have ghost writers, but there's a lot more that we can't do because we can't afford it. So we still have our lawyer and we still have our ghost writers, but we just do a lot more of that stuff. (00:59:27): And so we notice that. We start to then use ChatGPT and cloud first, these general purpose tools to try it and see is this useful? Does this actually work? All that kind of stuff. And then if it does, we will unbundle it into its own separate thing that becomes an app. And I think what's really special about this time is the entire game board has been totally reset in terms of things you can build. Where five years ago it was like you're going to build another Notes app. We've been building notes app for forever, another B2B SAS app. It's all the same stuff in slightly different packaging. And now it's totally new territory. No one knows what's going on. Everyone's inventing it as it happens. All these new workflows are being created in a very similar way to, I don't know, for example, when spreadsheets were first a thing on computers, we were figuring out all these new workflows on spreadsheets. (01:00:24): They got unbundled in the B2B SAS, same thing for ChatGPT and Claude. And what's really cool is you can be like, cool, I'm using using ChatGPT for this. It's really useful for me. And you might be one of the first people to really notice that. And then because everybody that works at Every is AI first and came to us because they reads Every, they read Every, so we all have the same vibe and we're all kind of doing similar stuff. They become our first users. So we measure the success of the product by is it a banger inside of Every, monologue the app that I was talking to you about, everyone just started using it and we're like, okay, we've got something here. (01:01:05): And what's really interesting then is if everyone inside of Every uses it and people read Every, they have a similar vibe to us too, so they become the next set of users. And that's a really, I think, interesting pipeline for building applications or building apps. It's a totally new greenfield so that all the stuff you're thinking about, it's probably new, which is really cool. And over time, what I think is organizations like ours, people who are playing at the edge, we're doing things that in three years everybody else is going to be doing. So it may be kind of niche for now, but it will be a big deal in three years when everyone else has the same needs that we do.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我很想谈谈我们如何看待构建产品，构建什么产品，我们最终构建什么？因为我认为它有一些特别之处，可能有一本对人们有用的剧本。所以当我想到......这只是最近才成为焦点。所以很多事情只是凭直觉做，没有真正考虑过。但当我想到我们最终孵化出的东西时，它基本上回到了我一开始所说的，那就是这些东西在历史上非常昂贵，只有富人或大公司才能购买。所以你的电子邮件的幕僚长，我认为治疗师或律师是另一个有趣的例子。另一个例子是有人整理你的衣柜或整理你的电脑。有人直接为你服务，价格变得便宜了几个数量级，这样即使你是一家小型初创公司，每个人都可以使用它们。 (00:58:39)：基本上，当你跑步时，我们就是一家人工智能优先的公司。你会遇到所有这些小事情，你会想，我希望我现在有一个代笔作家，但代笔作家真的很贵。或者我希望有一位律师，但这会花费我 25,000 美元。律师的费用确实很高，而且对这些服务的需求远远超出了能够满足的范围，因为它们是如此昂贵。人工智能的作用是让你觉得，哦，我可以使用云来实现这一点。我可以使用 ChatGPT 来实现这一点。因此，您可以利用您的要求，让我们聘请律师。我们有代笔作家，但还有很多事情我们不能做，因为我们负担不起。所以我们仍然有我们的律师，我们仍然有我们的代笔作家，但我们只是做了更多这样的事情。 (00:59:27)：我们注意到了这一点。我们首先开始使用ChatGPT和云，这些通用工具来尝试一下，看看这有用吗？这真的有效吗？所有这些东西。如果确实如此，我们将把它拆分成一个单独的东西，成为一个应用程序。我认为这次真正特别的是整个游戏板在你可以建造的东西方面已经完全重置。五年前，您似乎要构建另一个 Notes 应用程序。我们一直在构建笔记应用程序，这是另一个 B2B SAS 应用程序。都是相同的东西，但包装略有不同。现在这是一个全新的领域。没有人知道发生了什么事。每个人都在创造它。所有这些新的工作流程都是以非常相似的方式创建的，我不知道，例如，当电子表格首先出现在计算机上时，我们正在电子表格上找出所有这些新的工作流程。 (01:00:24)：他们在 B2B SAS 中被拆分，对于 ChatGPT 和 Claude 来说也是如此。真正酷的是，您可以说，酷，我正在使用 ChatGPT 来实现此目的。这对我来说真的很有用。您可能是第一批真正注意到这一点的人之一。然后因为在 Every 工作的每个人首先都是人工智能，他们来到我们这里是因为他们阅读 Every，他们阅读 Every，所以我们都有相同的氛围，我们都在做类似的事情。他们成为我们的第一批用户。因此，我们衡量产品成功与否的标准是它是否是我与您谈论的应用程序中的每个人的独白，每个人都刚刚开始使用它，我们就像，好吧，我们在这里有一些东西。 (01:01:05)：真正有趣的是，如果 Every 内部的每个人都使用它并且人们阅读 Every，他们也与我们有类似的氛围，所以他们成为下一组用户。我认为，这对于构建应用程序或构建应用程序来说确实是一个有趣的管道。这是一个全新的领域，所以你正在考虑的所有东西都可能是新的，这真的很酷。随着时间的推移，我认为像我们这样的组织，那些处于边缘的人，我们正在做的事情是其他人在三年内都会做的。因此，目前这可能是一种利基市场，但三年后，当其他人都有与我们相同的需求时，这将是一件大事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really cool. What I'm hearing is GPT wrappers are a good idea and are worth building.
turns.zh: 这真的很酷。我听说 GPT 包装器是个好主意，值得构建。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: 100% thank you. GPT wrappers are amazing and they've been much maligned for absolutely no reason and people don't understand how absolutely valuable they are.
turns.zh: 100%谢谢你。 GPT 包装器非常神奇，但它们却无缘无故地受到了很多诟病，人们不明白它们的绝对价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's also just you guys raised a sip seed round. This is a good time to maybe talk about that. Just these products don't have to become some mega-billion dollar hits. You kind of have this portfolio of companies, you have the content business. So I think there's a really interesting approach to how big these need to get to be successful. Maybe just talk about that.
turns.zh: 我想也只有你们筹集了种子轮资金。也许现在是谈论这个问题的好时机。这些产品不一定会成为价值数十亿美元的热门产品。你拥有这样的公司组合，你拥有内容业务。所以我认为有一个非常有趣的方法来确定这些公司需要多大才能成功。也许只是谈谈这个。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah. I really want Every to be an institution that teaches people how to live a better, more human life with technology, particularly with AI. And both teaches them how to do it with writing and the content we make and then builds tools for them to do that. But I think fundamental to building an institution is, at least for me, the way I would like to do it is I want internally it to feel like this creative playground where we have the opportunity to take risk and do stuff and do weird stuff that just doesn't make any sense. We can't justify anyone, but we just feel like it would be fun. And so I think I'm always playing with that dynamic tension between institution serious, we want this to be lasting and important and it should just be fun. Let's play around. And I think having that tension is really valuable. (01:03:16): And so I've always been sort of hesitant to raise a lot of money because I think it locks you into having to be that serious thing that's totally going for it. And there's lots of companies that figure out that balance. But just for me personally as a founder, I'm like, I want to keep the optionality alive and I want to keep the kind of playful feeling alive. And I think part of that comes from I know I have the control to do what I want more or less. There's probably also some deeper psychological things going on there, which I'm happy to talk about if you want to get into it. But I think there's also just... That's what I want. And so when we started Every, we raised a very small 700K pre-seed round, and this was at the height of the creator economy. (01:03:59): So we both started our newsletters. He and I started our newsletters around the same time. It was the hypest, craziest thing. People were throwing money around. It was wild. But we raised 700K because it was like, I want to raise enough for us to be able to experiment, have a little cash cushion, but not so much that it locks us into anything. And we sent an email to all of our investors being like, and you're one of our investors, so you've probably got this email.
turns.zh: 是的。我真的希望Every成为一个机构，教人们如何利用技术，特别是人工智能，过上更好、更人性化的生活。两者都教他们如何通过写作和我们制作的内容来做到这一点，然后为他们构建工具来做到这一点。但我认为建立一个机构的根本是，至少对我来说，我想要的方式是我希望在内部它感觉像一个创意游乐场，我们有机会冒险，做一些事情，做一些没有任何意义的奇怪的事情。我们无法为任何人辩护，但我们只是觉得这会很有趣。因此，我认为我总是在认真地处理机构之间的动态紧张关系，我们希望这种关系持久且重要，而且应该很有趣。我们来玩玩吧。我认为拥有这种紧张感真的很有价值。 (01:03:16)：所以我一直对筹集大量资金犹豫不决，因为我认为这会让你不得不成为那种完全投入的严肃的事情。有很多公司都找到了这种平衡。但就我个人而言，作为创始人，我想，我想保持选择性，我想保持那种有趣的感觉。我认为部分原因是我知道我有控制力去做我或多或少想做的事情。那里可能还存在一些更深层次的心理问题，如果您想了解的话，我很乐意谈论这些问题。但我认为还有...这就是我想要的。因此，当我们启动 Every 时，我们筹集了 70 万美元的种子前融资，当时正值创作者经济的鼎盛时期。 (01:03:59)：所以我们都开始发布时事通讯。他和我大约在同一时间开始了我们的时事通讯。这是最炒作、最疯狂的事情。人们到处乱扔钱。很狂野。但我们筹集了 70 万美元，因为我想筹集到足够的资金让我们能够进行实验，有一点现金缓冲，但又不能太多，以至于让我们陷入任何困境。我们向所有投资者发送了一封电子邮件，内容是，您是我们的投资者之一，所以您可能会收到这封电子邮件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tiny investor. But I'm in there, I'm in there.
turns.zh: 小投资者。但我就在那里，我就在那里。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: We sent an email to everyone being like, this is probably not a venture business, so you should not expect us to raise again. And we even raised on this slightly modified safe that gave everyone the option to convert to equity in three years, even if we didn't raise more money. So we did it in a way that allowed us the option to get really big and do the traditional thing and also the option to do it the way we want to do it. Maybe it's not a huge business, but we love it. That's great. And we did the same thing for this recent round where we raised up to 2 million from Reid Hoffman and starting line VC. And we did it as what I've been calling a sip seed round, which is basically they've committed $2 million, but we can pull it down whenever we want and we just do it on a safe at a set cap. (01:05:12): And for me, that's really helpful because it allows me psychologically to take a lot more risk. If we go to zero on the bank account, I can get more money. Great. I don't have to think about it. But what's also really helpful is I'm not, and the rest of the team is not staring at a gigantic number in the bank account being like, cool, we can burn this. Let's burn it. And also for our investors, I think Reid very much wants us to succeed, but I don't think he cares what size of business this is. I think he's more philosophically aligned with the thing that we're trying to do. And if it becomes a huge business, he's psyched for it. And I think that kind of alignment is what I was looking for. I think there's this core creative spirit to the thing that I want to maintain and I really care about having a big impact. (01:06:03): But I think there's a lot of ways to have an impact. And one of them is building a $10 billion business. I think another way is really changing how people see the world, see themselves in the world. And I think that's what stories do. And you don't necessarily... Sometimes you do that by building a gigantic company, but you don't necessarily always have to do that. A lot of the stories that we care about most are from people who maybe they weren't rich at all. And so I really like creating this place where we can make a really good business. And I care a lot about that. But also the core of the soul of it is about changing how people see themselves in the world.
turns.zh: 我们向每个人发送了一封电子邮件，内容是，这可能不是风险投资业务，因此您不应期望我们再次筹集资金。我们甚至在这个稍微修改过的保险箱上筹集资金，即使我们没有筹集更多资金，每个人都可以选择在三年内转换为股权。所以我们这样做的方式让我们可以选择变得更大并做传统的事情，也可以选择按照我们想要的方式来做。也许这不是一个大生意，但我们喜欢它。那太棒了。我们在最近的一轮融资中也做了同样的事情，从 Reid Hoffman 和 Starter Line VC 那里筹集了 200 万美元。我们这样做的方式就是我所说的种子轮融资，基本上他们已经承诺了 200 万美元，但我们可以随时撤资，而且我们只是在固定上限的安全范围内进行。 (01:05:12)：对我来说，这真的很有帮助，因为它让我在心理上可以承担更多的风险。如果我们的银行账户归零，我就能得到更多的钱。伟大的。我不必考虑它。但真正有用的是我没有，团队的其他成员也没有盯着银行账户中的巨大数字，说，酷，我们可以烧掉它。我们把它烧掉吧。对于我们的投资者来说，我认为里德非常希望我们成功，但我认为他并不关心我们的业务规模有多大。我认为他在哲学上更符合我们正在尝试做的事情。如果它成为一项巨大的业务，他就会对此感到兴奋。我认为这种一致性正是我所寻求的。我认为我想要维持的东西有这种核心的创造性精神，我真的很关心产生巨大的影响。 (01:06:03)：但我认为有很多方法可以产生影响。其中之一正在打造价值 100 亿美元的业务。我认为另一种方式正在真正改变人们看待世界、看待自己在世界上的方式。我认为这就是故事的作用。你不一定……有时你可以通过建立一家巨大的公司来做到这一点，但你不一定总是必须这样做。我们最关心的很多故事都来自那些可能根本不富有的人。所以我真的很喜欢创建这个地方，让我们可以做真正好的生意。我非常关心这一点。但其灵魂的核心是改变人们如何看待自己在世界上的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you've kind of innovated a new middle ground way of fundraising, not bootstrap and not just regular VC. It's a seed. And I love that this two... If I raised 50 million, it'd be like, okay, I get it. Let's not put 50 million in our bank account, but you do have 2 million. It's too much for us. We don't want to see that in our account.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你创新了一种新的中间地带筹款方式，而不是引导，也不仅仅是常规的风险投资。这是一颗种子。我喜欢这两个人……如果我筹集到 5000 万美元，那就会是，好吧，我明白了。我们的银行账户里没有5000万，但你有200万。这对我们来说太多了。我们不想在我们的帐户中看到这种情况。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: That's another thing. And we'll see how this ages. I might be back here in two years crying the blues because we didn't raise enough money or whatever. Who knows? But that's the other thing is I do think we can get so much further with very small amounts of money. Like Cora, I think all in to build Cora, we've spent maybe 300K, Maybe. That's crazy because-
turns.zh: 那是另一回事了。我们会看看它是如何老化的。两年后我可能会因为我们没有筹集到足够的资金或其他原因而回到这里哭泣。谁知道？但另一件事是我确实认为我们可以用很少的钱走得更远。就像 Cora 一样，我认为为了构建 Cora，我们可能花费了 30 万美元。这太疯狂了，因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that includes salaries?
turns.zh: 这包括工资吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Includes salaries. Yeah.
turns.zh: 包括工资。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: This product was not even technically possible even if you had billions of dollars three years ago. Not possible because you can't do email summarizing and automatic responses and all that kind of stuff without GPT. So not only was it totally impossible, but now we can get with two engineers, we can get the amount done that would've taken a team of 20 people. And I think that means that we need less money. And I don't think that VC has really caught up to that yet. And I think there are other companies that are doing... There's a term called seed strapping, so there are other companies that are starting to wake up to this too. And I'm curious about how it changes the VC model. For sure for us, we have a specific incubation model, which is a bit different from a VC model. And I think there's some differentiation in the stuff that we can do with founders, which is kind of cool. But yeah, I'm just trying to figure out a shape that works for me and that's different from other people and we'll see how this goes.
turns.zh: 即使三年前你有数十亿美元，这个产品在技术上也是不可能实现的。不可能，因为如果没有 GPT，您就无法进行电子邮件摘要和自动回复以及所有此类操作。因此，这不仅是完全不可能的，而且现在我们可以通过两名工程师完成需要 20 人团队才能完成的工作。我认为这意味着我们需要更少的钱。我认为风险投资还没有真正赶上这一点。我认为还有其他公司正在做……有一个术语叫做“种子捆绑”，所以其他公司也开始意识到这一点。我很好奇它如何改变风险投资模式。对于我们来说，可以肯定的是，我们有一个特定的孵化模式，这与 VC 模式有点不同。我认为我们可以与创始人做一些不同的事情，这很酷。但是，是的，我只是想找出一种适合我的形状，并且与其他人不同，我们会看看效果如何。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll revisit in a couple years. Seems like it's going great from the outside. I'm going to ask about a couple other things before we wrap up. One is around this consulting arm that you have. I think it's really interesting because like I said, I feel like this could be a billion-dollar business. I feel like every company right now is trying to figure out what the hell's everyone else figured out that we're not doing. I've had so many emails from chief product officers at companies being like, can you introduce me to some chief product officers that have done cool things with AI that we should learn from? So many people and I would just introduce them to each other and it's cool because you guys are basically solving that problem for a lot of companies. (01:09:18): So one is just maybe share a bit about what that side of the business for folks. And then two, I feel like I imagine you've seen companies that have done this really well, have adopted AI, things have worked really well, they found really good productivity gains, and then you found companies that don't. What do you find is the difference between those two?
turns.zh: 我们将在几年后再次访问。从外面看似乎进展顺利。在结束之前我要问一些其他的事情。其中之一是围绕您拥有的咨询部门。我认为这真的很有趣，因为就像我说的，我觉得这可能是一项价值十亿美元的业务。我觉得现在每家公司都在试图弄清楚其他人都知道但我们没有做的事情。我收到了很多来自公司首席产品官的电子邮件，比如，你能给我介绍一些在人工智能方面做出了很酷的事情的首席产品官吗？我们应该向他们学习？我和很多人只是将他们互相介绍，这很酷，因为你们基本上正在为很多公司解决这个问题。 (01:09:18)：所以我们可能只是分享一下这方面的业务对人们来说意味着什么。然后第二点，我觉得你已经看到公司在这方面做得非常好，采用了人工智能，事情进展得非常好，他们发现生产力确实得到了很好的提高，然后你发现了一些公司没有这样做。您发现这两者之间有什么区别？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: I love this question and I have a very specific opinion about this. So one, yeah, the consulting arm, basically we spend all of our time playing around with new models, writing about them and building stuff with them. And we have a big audience. So naturally we've gotten companies over time being like, can you just come and teach us how to do this? And so we started to do that. This is pretty nascent. It's probably been over the last six to nine months, but it's a pretty big business now. It'll probably double this year. Last year we did about a million. Maybe it'll be more this year. We'll see. It depends on a couple... We have a couple of big contracts out, so it might be way more than that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题，并且对此有非常具体的看法。所以，是的，咨询部门，基本上我们把所有的时间都花在研究新模型上，写下它们并用它们构建东西。我们有很多观众。因此，随着时间的推移，我们很自然地得到了一些公司，比如，你能过来教我们如何做到这一点吗？所以我们开始这样做。这是相当新生的。这可能已经过去六到九个月了，但现在它是一项相当大的生意。今年可能会翻倍。去年我们做了大约一百万。也许今年会更多。我们拭目以待。这取决于几个……我们有几份大合同，所以可能远不止于此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A billion. I predict a billion dollars in a few years.
turns.zh: 十亿。我预计几年后将达到十亿美元。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: But yeah, basically people are like, can you come help us learn how to do this? So what we do is we spend some time going and researching your organization. So we go in and try to understand what are all the different teams doing, what are the repetitive tasks, some of the stuff we were talking about earlier. And then what we will do is first we present a little report, tells you here's everything that we found. Here's not only that, but you have a chatbot where you can chat with all the interviews that we did and you can pull out your own insights. We have a whole dashboard where it shows you, here are the teams that are really into this, here are the teams that are not. Here's how much leverage you might be able to get on different teams based on the interviews and based on the AI analysis. (01:10:57): It's pretty cool. And that's an app that I coded over a weekend with Devin a year ago. And then Alex runs part of the consulting has helped upgrade it. Then what we do is we have a training curriculum. So we go in and train each team and we customize it based on the interviews that we do. Because one of the interesting things about AI is it's such a general purpose technology, and I think people who work inside companies, 10% of them are like, I'm super curious about this. 10% are like, I will never touch this. And 80% are like, if you tell me how to do it for my job, I'll do it. (01:11:31): And so we customize the training to be like, here are the exact prompts you're going to use and here's the exact situations you're going to use them. And that really, I think helps drive the adoption. We spend four weeks with each team, an hour a week, that kind of thing. It seems to be really cool. And then we'll often also after this, go and build automations and do some of the AI operations stuff we were talking about earlier. Companies really like it. I think we work with a lot of big hedge funds and PE firms and big companies, all that kind of stuff. To your-
turns.zh: 但是，是的，基本上人们会说，你能来帮助我们学习如何做到这一点吗？因此，我们所做的就是花一些时间去研究您的组织。因此，我们深入了解所有不同团队在做什么，重复性任务是什么，以及我们之前讨论过的一些内容。然后我们要做的就是首先提交一份小报告，告诉您这是我们发现的所有内容。不仅如此，您还有一个聊天机器人，您可以在其中与我们进行的所有采访进行聊天，并且可以得出您自己的见解。我们有一个完整的仪表板，它向您显示，这里是真正热衷于此的团队，这里是不热衷于此的团队。根据访谈和人工智能分析，您可以在不同的团队中获得多少影响力。 (01:10:57)：这非常酷。这是我一年前与 Devin 一起在周末编写的一个应用程序。然后亚历克斯运行的部分咨询帮助升级了它。然后我们要做的就是制定培训课程。因此，我们进去培训每个团队，并根据我们所做的采访进行定制。因为人工智能的一个有趣之处在于它是一种通用技术，我认为在公司内部工作的人，其中 10％ 的人会说，我对此非常好奇。 10% 的人会说，我永远不会碰这个。 80% 的人会说，如果你告诉我如何做我的工作，我就会做。 (01:11:31)：因此我们将培训定制为：以下是您将使用的确切提示，以下是您将使用它们的具体情况。我认为这确实有助于推动采用。我们和每个团队待了四个星期，每周一个小时，诸如此类。看起来真的很酷。然后我们通常也会在此之后构建自动化并执行我们之前讨论的一些人工智能操作。公司真的很喜欢它。我认为我们与很多大型对冲基金、私募股权公司和大公司等等合作。给你的——

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Companies, all that kind of stuff. To your second question, which is, "What separates the good companies from the bad, or the companies that end up adopting this?," I think the number one predictor is, "Does the CEO use ChatGPT?," or insert your own chatbot. If the CEO is in it all the time, being like, "This is the coolest thing," everybody else is going to start doing it. If the CEO is like, "I don't know, this is for someone else," no one else is going to be able to lead that charge, and they're either going to have ... Either they're going to be negative on it, and so definitely no one's going to do it, or they're going to have way unrealistic expectations because they have no intuition for what's possible, and they're just going to get really disappointed. (01:12:47): But the CEOs that are using it all the time are able to both drive the excitement and set reasonable expectations for what can be achieved, and so those things end up working really well, and the people that do this really well ... So, for example, we work with a hedge fund called Walleye, which I had the founder on my podcast, AI and I, a few weeks ago, their gigantic $10 billion hedge fund. One of the things that they do, which I think they're basically the model for how to do this, first thing you did, which a lot of CEOs are doing is send the, "We're an AI-first company" email. Everyone's got the memo. (01:13:20): You just got to really do it, and one of the things he said in his memo, which I love, is, "I wrote this email with ChatGPT, and you should too." So you got to like ...
turns.zh: 公司，诸如此类的东西。对于你的第二个问题，即“好公司与坏公司的区别，或者最终采用这种技术的公司的区别是什么？”，我认为第一个预测因素是，“首席执行官是否使用 ChatGPT？”或者插入你自己的聊天机器人。如果首席执行官一直参与其中，说“这是最酷的事情”，那么其他人就会开始这样做。如果首席执行官说，“我不知道，这是给别人的”，那么其他人就无法领导这项工作，他们要么......要么他们对此持消极态度，所以肯定没有人会这样做，要么他们会有不切实际的期望，因为他们对可能发生的事情没有直觉，他们只会感到非常失望。 (01:12:47)：但一直在使用它的首席执行官能够既激发兴奋感，又对可以实现的目标设定合理的期望，因此这些事情最终运作得非常好，而那些做得非常好的人......所以，例如，我们与一家名为 Walleye 的对冲基金合作，几周前，我在我的播客上邀请了其创始人 AI 和我，他们的 100 亿美元的庞大对冲基金。他们所做的事情之一，我认为他们基本上是如何做到这一点的模型，你做的第一件事，很多首席执行官正在做的就是发送“我们是一家人工智能优先的公司”电子邮件。每个人都有备忘录。 (01:13:20)：你必须真正做到这一点，我喜欢他在备忘录中所说的其中一件事，就是“我用 ChatGPT 写了这封电子邮件，你也应该这么做。”所以你必须喜欢...

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the memo.
turns.zh: 在备忘录中。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah. You got to lead from the front in that way. And then, what he does in, I think what a lot of other really cool companies do is they're doing weekly meetings where people share prompts and share use cases. They do a weekly email to their entire company, being like, "Okay, here are our usage stats for ChatGPT. Here are the people that came up with a new prompt and contributed to it." (01:14:00): Create this sort of awareness and momentum, because going back to the point I made earlier, about 10% of people are early adopters, those are the people inside of a company that you need to find and highlight because they're going to just go spend all this time figuring out what works, and then all you have to do is translate what they learn into the rest of the organization. And so if you create forums for them to be rewarded, you're going to automatically transfer a lot of their learnings to everybody else, and encourage more of it, and I think that's kind of the secret.
turns.zh: 是的。你必须以这种方式从前线领导。然后，我认为许多其他非常酷的公司所做的就是他们每周举行会议，人们在会上分享提示并分享用例。他们每周向整个公司发送一封电子邮件，内容如下：“好吧，这是我们的 ChatGPT 使用统计数据。这是提出新提示并为其做出贡献的人。” (01:14:00)：创造这种意识和动力，因为回到我之前提出的观点，大约 10% 的人是早期采用者，这些人是你需要找到并突出显示的公司内部人员，因为他们会花所有时间找出有效的方法，然后你所要做的就是将他们学到的知识转化为组织的其他人员。因此，如果你创建论坛让他们获得奖励，你就会自动将他们的很多知识转移给其他人，并鼓励更多人这样做，我认为这就是秘密。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is awesome. I love this advice. So just to reflect back, what you just shared, a few kind of tactics you find that you encourage within companies, one is just send this memo, the Toby memo. I don't know if that's the right way to describe it, who I think it was first along these lines just, "We're AI-first." It's going to be part of your performance review. (01:14:50): It's going to be asking, "Can you do it in AI before you could talk to anyone else?," all these things, and then just note, "I wrote this using ChatGPT's," it's a great idea. This idea of a weekly meeting, so it's like a live or Zoom meeting, where people share, "Here's the thing I've learned about using AI," and then this weekly stats email of, "Here's how much we're using ChatGPT across the org. Here's some people that did some awesome work."
turns.zh: 那太棒了。我喜欢这个建议。所以，回顾一下，你刚才分享的内容，你发现你在公司内部鼓励的几种策略，其中之一就是发送这份备忘录，托比备忘录。我不知道这是否是描述它的正确方式，我认为这是第一个这样的说法，“我们是人工智能第一。”这将成为你绩效评估的一部分。 (01:14:50)：它会问，“在与其他人交谈之前，你能在人工智能中做到这一点吗？”所有这些事情，然后只需注意，“我用 ChatGPT 写了这个，”这是一个好主意。每周会议的想法，所以它就像现场或 Zoom 会议，人们在会上分享，“这是我学到的关于使用人工智能的东西”，然后每周统计电子邮件，“这是我们在整个组织中使用 ChatGPT 的程度。这里有一些人做了一些很棒的工作。”

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And I especially love this very simple heuristic of, "If you're a CEO, uses ChatGPT or Claude, or whatever daily, it's going to work out."
turns.zh: 惊人的。我特别喜欢这个非常简单的启发式，“如果你是首席执行官，每天使用 ChatGPT 或 Claude，或者其他任何东西，它就会成功。”

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. I know it's early, but what kind of impact have you seen from a company, kind of leaning into this and adopting AI widely? Anything you've seen either anecdotally or numbers-wise?
turns.zh: 那太酷了。我知道现在还为时过早，但是您从公司中看到了什么样的影响，有哪些倾向并广泛采用人工智能？您从轶事或数字上看到过什么吗？

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: It's early. It's really hard to say other than ... I think generally, people who do this well now feel like they can do way more work than they used to without having to hire more people, and so they're just going further faster at the same budget. I don't see a lot of people being like, "Cool. We're going to fire a bunch of people." (01:15:58): Also, I don't really want to do consulting work like that. That sucks. But we've never had to say no. Mostly, people are like, "Cool. I'm just going to go further with the people that I have." (01:16:08): I think also, back to kind of the first point I made about reshoring American jobs, I have seen some companies, not the ones that we worked with, but I have seen some companies of people that I'm friends with, where they're like, "We have a call center somewhere, but I think I can get the same amount done with two employees in the U.S. that use one of these customer service platforms." They're still not totally automatic. I think that Klarna CEO thing, that was bullshit. But, yeah, you can have a couple people in the U.S. that maybe you pay a little bit less to than you would for 100 people somewhere else, and obviously, that's the calculus that everyone has to make for themselves, but I've definitely seen that happen, and yeah, I think that's the get more done with the same amount of people.
turns.zh: 现在还早。真的很难说，除了......我认为一般来说，做得好的人现在感觉他们可以比以前做更多的工作，而不必雇用更多的人，所以他们只是在相同的预算下走得更快。我没有看到很多人会说，“酷。我们要解雇一群人。” (01:15:58)：另外，我真的不想做那样的咨询工作。太糟糕了。但我们从来不必说不。大多数情况下，人们会说，“酷。我只是要和我拥有的人一起走得更远。” (01:16:08)：我也认为，回到我关于回流美国就业机会的第一点，我见过一些公司，不是我们合作过的公司，但我见过一些我是朋友的公司，他们会说，“我们在某个地方有一个呼叫中心，但我认为我可以通过使用这些客户服务平台之一的美国两名员工完成同样的工作。”它们仍然不是完全自动的。我认为 Klarna 首席执行官的事完全是胡说八道。但是，是的，你可以在美国为几个人支付比在其他地方为 100 个人支付的费用要少一些，显然，这是每个人都必须为自己做的计算，但我确实看到了这种情况的发生，是的，我认为这就是用相同数量的人做更多的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe to close out our conversation, I want to come back to this idea that you referenced, but I want to spend a little more time on this, which is this idea of the allocation economy. If I understand it correctly, we've been in this knowledge economy, where people get paid to do a thing, and your thesis is that we're moving to this allocation economy, where the manager skills become more important, and we're going to be spending more of our time managing. And I think what's amazing about this is it also tells you which skills will matter more in the future, which is something I think a lot of people are thinking about. So maybe just answer that question and share whatever you think is important to share to give people a sense of what you're thinking.
turns.zh: 也许为了结束我们的谈话，我想回到你提到的这个想法，但我想花更多的时间在这上面，这就是分配经济的想法。如果我理解正确的话，我们一直处于知识经济时代，人们做某事就可以获得报酬，而你的论点是我们正在转向分配经济，管理者的技能变得更加重要，我们将花更多的时间进行管理。我认为这令人惊奇的是它还告诉你哪些技能在未来会更重要，我认为这是很多人都在考虑的事情。因此，也许只需回答这个问题并分享您认为重要的任何内容，以便让人们了解您的想法。

turns.speaker: Dan Shipper
turns.en: Yeah. So this is based on our article I wrote two, two and a half years ago. So this is back before agents were even thought of as viable. And I was really trying to think about, "How do I express what ... In my experience, using this every day, what skills are useful for me?," because I think that'll be the case for a lot of other people, and I think that's kind of the best method, I think, to do these sorts of predictions, is you have to be doing it all the time yourself, and then that informs your opinion about this stuff. (01:18:14): So what I noticed using, at the time, like GPT-3 or maybe GPT-4, was that I was spending a lot of time, for example, thinking about, "How do I communicate the problem? How do I gather the right information for the problem? How do I put it in the right way so that the model that I'm working with gets it? How do I pick which model to give it to you, and how do I maybe divide up the task to be like, 'Okay, this model does this, this model does this,' based on what I know to be like, 'What's good and what's bad?'? How do I give them feedback?" (01:18:50): "How do I have a vision for what I want and a set of criteria for whether it's good?" All that stuff is exactly how I found myself using these tools, and I was like, "Oh, that's just managing." And once that clicks for you, I think you'll start to see a lot of other things. So a really good example is there's a big complaint that it's like, "Well, how can I have AI do this? I can't trust that they're going to do it well, so I just do it myself." (01:19:22): And I'm just like, "Yeah, that's exactly what Every first-time manager says." You always have this problem, where you're like, "Okay. Well, if I delegate it, it's not done in the way that I want it to be done. If I do it myself, I get no leverage." And so that's how a manager has to learn how to be a manager is like, "When do I lean in and maybe micromanage a little bit, and when can I delegate, and how can I trust it, and how do I divide up the task and all that kind of stuff?" (01:19:45): And so I think there's a lot of overlap in those skills. And those skills are not broadly distributed right now, but they will be in the future because it will be so much cheaper to be a manager.

If you're a citizen, generalist. You could be expected to be a fighter, a judge, a juror, maybe a general. turns.zh: 但我认为人工智能对我来说如此出色的原因之一是我喜欢涉足不同的事物。所以就像有一天，我可以编写一个应用程序、制作视频、制作图像、写作以及所有类似的事情，而 ChatGPT 就在我身边。我认为，随着文明从古希腊发展到现在，我们发现，我们的专业化程度越高，我们就越能更好地在许多不同的人之间进行协调。就像亚当·斯密（Adam Smith）一样，有一家别针工厂，有人在制造别针或其他什么东西，这是针对我们行业的专业化。这产生了很多非常好的影响。 (01:21:18)：我最喜欢的例子之一是回到古希腊、古雅典。雅典是一个多面手的文明，至少对公民来说是这样。他们与妇女和奴隶有着不好的历史，但我们先把它放在一边。如果你是公民，通才。你可能会成为一名战士、一名法官、一名陪审员，甚至可能是一名将军。 (01:21:46)：您可以预期它在您的一生中会在您的社会中扮演许多不同的角色。但情况发生了变化，因为雅典成为了一个帝国。当它成为一个帝国时，如果你要派一位将军去入侵西西里岛或其他地方，你希望那个人非常熟练。所以它开始把一般的事情分解成人们开始扮演特定的角色，他们相互协调以及诸如此类的事情，我认为这种模式实际上对发展文明非常有好处，但从很多方面来说，它也不那么有趣。成为一个全面发展的人实际上真的很酷。我认为人工智能的有趣之处在于，它有点像，你可以把它想象成你的口袋里有 10,000 个博士学位。 (01:22:36)：它对人类知识的每一个小分支、每一种艺术形式以及每一种制造事物或建造事物的方式都了解得很多，而你只是能够接触到这些，所以它正在做很多……这对完成很多专门的任务很有好处，而你可能需要花 10 年才能擅长了解这种特定的蝉种类，这样你就可以确切地知道它们是如何繁殖的。但现在，你口袋里有了这个东西，它可以在任何给定的情况下、任何给定的时间告诉你所有信息，因此你能够在所有不同的技能领域之间进行更多的跳跃，并且你可以做更多的事情，例如，像创始人一样，我认为我们可以在 15 人的情况下保持比我们能够做的更长的时间。因此，Every 内部的人可以在更长时间内保持通才，我认为这可能会波及到经济的其他领域，在经济的其他领域，而不是巨大的、大规模的公司，每个人都在做一个小小的按钮转动，你有更多更小的组织，有更多的通才，我认为这实际上是一件好事。
