turns.en: I think generally, when you're building a company, even if you do it the way that I do it or did it, which is you don't raise a lot of money and you try to stay in control, there's a big temptation to try to run the company in the way you think you should. And I have this weird thing where I'm like, "I really love writing, but I also really love business," and there were not a lot of models for me of people who had successful businesses that were also writers. It turns out there are, but I didn't know about that for a while. And so early on at Every, it was growing really well, because I was writing a lot, and Nathan was writing a lot. And when I stopped writing, the business didn't work as well because media businesses don't follow the same pattern as tech startups, because if you're a media business and you are a founder who then hires people to make the product, which is right, if you have product market fit before, you lose it, and maybe you hire people that are good writers, but that's hard. It's total opposite pattern for startups. So you build the first version of the product, and then you hire people to build the rest of it, and so that's what I did. And I also really struggled with, "Okay, what are the implications for that and for my career," and I think it was hard for me to admit, like I actually want to write because I just didn't have any examples of someone being the kind of writer that I wanted to be. And what's really interesting is three years into the business ... The business has been pretty flat. (01:30:57): I was pretty miserable because I was not doing the thing that I really wanted to do, and I asked ChatGPT, I was like, "Are there any examples of writers that have built businesses?" And it was like, "Yeah, Joel Spolsky, who built Trello and Stack Overflow. There's Jason Fried who I've known for a long time, and I've always looked up to, but I forgot about in this context. There is Sam Harris who's got a great podcast, and he's got a gigantic meditation app. There is Bill Simmons, who's incredible podcaster and also built The Ringer, sold to Spotify for a couple hundred million bucks. (01:31:32): There's a lot of these people, and there are patterns that they use to build companies that are pretty well-understood. They're just not typical Silicon Valley patterns. And so I was like, "Cool. I just want to be a writer. I think it'll be really fun." (01:31:48): And so I sort of flipped. I still have the builder, entrepreneur, founder part of my identity, but I sort of flipped it to be like writing is at the center, and I'm unapologetic about it, and that's actually good for the business. It's good for me and it's good for the business. And the more I've leaned into that, doing the thing that ... If you told anyone that you're starting a business, where it's like, "Well, we're going to be a newsletter, and we're going to incubate all these apps, and we're going to do consulting and whatever," they would be like, "You're nuts." (01:32:14): "Everyone wants to do that. Of course, Every founder wants to do that, but you have to focus. You can't write, whatever." But every time I've kind of just leaned into something that feels like the most, the ultimate luxury of my hidden secret desire, it's actually worked a lot better, and I think you end up ... What it really is, is there's a huge tax to doing something every day that you don't quite like that much, or you're not quite a fit for, and by sort of giving into those secret desires, you end up finding a shape for the work that you do and the business that you build that is good for you, and that's always going to be a somewhat unique shape from other businesses that have been built. (01:32:54): It's always going to rhyme with other things, but I think finding that unique shape, instead of just kind of cargo culting, like what you think a company should look like is definitely a much better way to be successful, and it's also a much better way to live.
turns.zh: 我认为一般来说，当你建立一家公司时，即使你按照我的方式去做，即你没有筹集很多资金并且你试图保持控制，仍然存在很大的诱惑，试图以你认为应该的方式经营公司。我有一个奇怪的事情，我就像，“我真的很喜欢写作，但我也真的很喜欢商业”，对于我来说，那些拥有成功企业同时也是作家的人的榜样并不多。事实证明是有的，但我有一段时间不知道。在Every早期，它发展得非常好，因为我写了很多，内森也写了很多。当我停止写作时，业务运作得不太好，因为媒体业务不遵循与科技初创公司相同的模式，因为如果你是一家媒体公司，你是一位创始人，然后雇用人员来制造产品，这是正确的，如果你之前有适合市场的产品，你就会失去它，也许你会雇用优秀作家的人，但这很难。对于初创公司来说，这是完全相反的模式。因此，您构建了产品的第一个版本，然后雇用人员来构建其余部分，这就是我所做的。我也真的很挣扎，“好吧，这对我的职业生涯有什么影响，”我想我很难承认，就像我真的想写作一样，因为我没有任何例子表明某人是我想成为的那种作家。真正有趣的是三年来......业务一直相当平淡。 (01:30:57)：我非常痛苦，因为我没有做我真正想做的事情，我问 ChatGPT，我想，“有没有什么作家创办了企业的例子？”就像是，“是的，Joel Spolsky，他创建了 Trello 和 Stack Overflow。还有 Jason Fried，我认识很久了，我一直很尊敬他，但我在这个背景下忘记了。还有 Sam Harris，他有一个很棒的播客，他有一个巨大的冥想应用程序。还有 Bill Simmons，他是一位令人难以置信的播客，还创建了 The Ringer，以几亿美元的价格卖给了 Spotify。 (01:31:32)：这样的人有很多，他们用来建立公司的模式是非常容易理解的，但他们并不是典型的硅谷模式。我只想成为一名作家。我认为这真的很有趣。” (01:31:48)：所以我有点翻转。我的身份中仍然有建设者、企业家、创始人的一部分，但我有点翻转它，就像写作是中心，我对此毫无歉意，这实际上对业务有好处。这对我有好处，对业务也有好处。而且我越倾向于这一点，做的事情......如果你告诉任何人当你开始创业时，他们会说，“好吧，我们将成为一份时事通讯，我们将孵化所有这些应用程序，我们将提供咨询服务等等，”他们会说，“你疯了。”(01:32:14)：“每个人都想这样做。当然，每个创始人都想这样做，但你必须集中精力。无论如何，你不会写。”但每次我只是倾向于某种感觉最棒的东西，我隐藏的秘密欲望的终极奢侈，它实际上效果更好，我认为你最终......它的真正含义是，每天做一些你不太喜欢的事情，或者你不太适合，并且通过屈服于这些秘密欲望，你最终会找到一种适合你所做的工作和业务的形状，你建立的东西对你有好处，而且它总是会与其他已经建立的企业有某种独特的形状（01:32:54）：它总是会与其他事物押韵，但我认为找到这种独特的形状，而不是像你认为的公司应该是什么样子那样只是一种货物崇拜，这绝对是一种更好的成功方式，也是一种更好的生活方式。
